questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to try to live in a completely different country far away, which didn't have the main language English. For me I had never been to Korea, and knew very little about the country, but I had heard good things, so that's why I chose it.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really enjoyed my stay in this amazing country. There was always more to see and the food was great. People were sweet. I can only recommend choosing Korea for exchange.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy, because I had gotten an email on which bus to take through my dorm  - International House - also download navermap (instead of google maps). It will show the way and offer all the public transportation possibilities. I took out some cash at the airport and bought a simcard, all of which one could have probably done cheaper from home. Then I bought the bus ticket and found it outside the airport.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I got to live at the university dorms. There were two - International House (only common rooms and for girls) and SK Global House. I lived in International House, and when I arrived there was a reception where I got a key-card and could ask questions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I had gotten a lot of emails with information and I was overall well-informed.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were two dorms - International House (girls, common rooms) and SK Global House (double room, single room, boys and girls). I lived in International House, since it was easier to get a spot so I applied there. Both options are very cheap, but to get for example a single room in SK Global it's very competitive and you have to almost push the apply button the second application opens.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There was a common kitchen on the first floor. Often there were a lot of people during dinner time, so I mostly ate out and had some lunch and breakfast sometimes at the dorms. Refrigerators were shared and it was a bit small with space. Also there are no kitchen supplies, so you have to buy your own pots, pans, utensils, soap etc. You can get this cheaply at the store Daiso.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: You have to be prepared to live with a roomie, if you apply for a common room. They might not have the same sleep schedule. The good things about the dorms is that it's cheap, easy housing and you can walk to class in ten minutes. The facilities at International House were newly renovated so the bathrooms and showers were great and the room were nice, the beds were a bit hard though and I had to get used to sleeping in the same room as a roomie. Also I found my friends through the dorms, because we arrived 4 days before uni introduction, so we had already gotten to know each other a bit. They also lived at the dorms, so it was always very convenient to meet up and get dinner etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I highly recommend the dorms if you want something easy and convenient close by campus. But you have to get used to small rooms and a roomie (except if you apply for a single rooms ofc.).

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was a bit complicated, but they send you a lot of information that you can read through.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You got some points that you could bid on courses with, and some courses can be a bit competitive. You have to look at the older years bidding averages to get a feel for how much to bid.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: We got information through mails. It is a bit complicated, so you have to read up on it.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I did bid too many points on the wrong courses, so there was one course I didn't get. Another course they didn't have my semester, that I thought they would have. I only took specific study abroad classes, so they were pretty easy to get into though. Also I was on exchange on my masters, but since I hadn't completed a full year I was called a 'senior', which meant I could only take one graduate course and the rest was undergraduate. This will also be written in the information you get.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Read up on the proces. Also have in mind that you can also take tennis, taekwondo, dance or Korean classes if you have enough points for it, and Copenhagen University will allow it. It just won't be on your final exam paper. The physical activities only counted as 1 point.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I liked the academic programme, but many of the courses were not relevant for public health. So please look this up beforehand, since it can be difficult to take classes other than the 'study abroad classes' which are more generalist classes with Korean history, politics and philosophy. As a public health student I did take a graduate course called Bio-security, which I can highly recommend.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I was a master student but since I hadn't passed a full year, I could only become a 'senior student', which meant I had to take undergraduate courses and could only take one master course.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was more high school style where you had to be there to get points for either participation or to avoid getting absence. Also you had to be more active in class and do presentations and assignments during the semester.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Law and justice, Ecology of human development, Traditional korean society and modernization, Korea-US relations, Bio-security, (+tennis).

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed Bio-security, which was my graduate courses. We were a small class with a passionate teacher.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did eat out a lot. If you eat at restaurants it's going to be 50-80 kr each time and if you eat at e-marts (like 7-eleven) it's going to be cheaper, but also just mostly instant ramen or gimbaps/onigiri. Also there is really good and cheap food at the cafeterias at uni which will be approximately 30 kr.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Eating out got expensive because I did it a lot.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There was a student fair where you could sign up to things. I didn't really engage since I already had tennis class. I did try to sign up to mountain climbing, but I didn't get a spot. There is a lot of opportunity though if you search for it.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were soccer, fencing, board games, climbing, dancing, language, band, tennis club, table tennis, lacrosse etc. There were a whole fair with clubs, that you could sign up to, but I don't remember all of them.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would have tried climbing if I had gotten in. I didn't engage a lot in these activities, but they looked fun.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: You can go on small trips - I did Busan, Suwon and then I also went to Taiwan. There is also a lot of small markets around in Seoul and tourist spots that are good to visit. I also went to Hongdae and Itaewon to dance and drink a few drinks.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it easy. People are very sweet and polite, and also very used to foreigners since there is still a lot of american soldiers stationed in Korea + there it tourists.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Sign up for the student clubs, because they most often also have social events with food and beers.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I think for me I mostly had to get used to living at a dorm with a roomie. Other than that I don't really know.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food, the kind people, all the things you could go see.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Read up on the courses available and the bidding system. Remember to get a TOEFL-test, if they still require it. Also I had to get a Tuberculosis test and certification to live at my dorm. I don't know if these are the most important things though. Maybe just remember to have fun. Many people travelled a lot, but I found it a bit stressful, because I also just wanted to enjoy the exchange experience. So don't stress about it and do what you feel like.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Eat at the good cafeterias at uni.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing a new culture and getting a little break and distance from your own life. Using this opportunity to try random hobbies and just do what I feel like.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It felt a bit strange and lonely at first, because it was so far away from everything. Just let it pass and try to enjoy, it will be fine.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
